strengths: The paper builds a genuinely rigorous real-analytic framework (with substantial appendix machinery) to prove almost-sure injectivity of decoder-only Transformers at the last-token representation, and further proves this property is preserved after any finite number of GD/SGD steps -- a nontrivial extension beyond prior initialization-only injectivity results (e.g., Sutter et al. 2025).

The theoretical claims are operationalized via SIPIT, a concrete, provably correct (a.s.), linear-time (Theta(T|V|)) algorithm for exact prompt reconstruction from hidden states, which is a useful and novel contribution distinct from prior approximate inversion methods that rely on trained inverters and black-box logits/logprobs.

Extensive empirical validation: billions of pairwise collision checks across six models (GPT-2, Gemma-3, Llama, Mistral, Phi-4, TinyStories), an exhaustive worst-case search over closest-prefix continuations (343B+ pairs per model), and sequence-length/depth ablations, all consistent with the theory and showing no collisions.

Clear comparisons against reasonable baselines (HardPrompts, brute force) showing SIPIT achieves exact recovery far more efficiently, and a careful, well-organized related-work section situating the contribution relative to both theoretical (surjectivity/injectivity) and applied (inversion) literature.
Strong reproducibility: detailed proofs, pseudocode, implementation details, and a stated commitment to release code with fixed seeds.
weaknesses: The theorems are stated over real-valued parameters and real-analytic functions, but real deployed LLMs run in finite-precision floating point (fp16/bf16/int8/int4), where the continuous-measure/probability-zero argument is not literally applicable; the paper's "failure cases" discussion of quantization is brief and does not adequately reconcile this gap with the strong practical/legal claims made in the discussion (e.g., "there is no free privacy once data enters a Transformer").

SIPIT requires full white-box access to model weights and the ability to compute forward (and backward) passes at a chosen layer; the privacy/legal framing in the discussion somewhat overstates real-world risk, since attackers who already have this level of access typically also have the input or don't need hidden-state inversion.

The runtime is technically linear in sequence length but scales with vocabulary size |V|, which is large (30k-250k) for modern LLMs; the only wall-clock inversion experiments are on GPT-2 Small (vocab ~50k), and it is unclear how SIPIT would scale to larger, modern models with bigger vocabularies and deeper stacks, despite these models being used for the (cheaper) collision-search experiments.

The core theoretical novelty is incremental relative to Sutter et al. (2025), who already establish almost-sure injectivity of the full hidden-state matrix at initialization; this paper's main technical additions are restricting to the last-token map and extending to training dynamics, which, while valuable, is a narrower delta than the framing ("Language Models are Injective and Hence Invertible") suggests.

The empirical collision search, while large-scale, is fundamentally a sanity check consistent with (rather than a stringent test of) the theory, since true adversarial or near-degenerate parameter regions are unlikely to be sampled by random prompts; the exhaustive test is restricted to only the 10 closest prefixes per model, which is a small and somewhat cherry-picked stress test.

Baseline comparisons (HardPrompts) are adapted from a different (multimodal, CLIP-based) setting rather than a like-for-like inversion baseline, which may make the comparison less informative about SIPIT's relative advantage against methods actually designed for this text-only setting.

strengths: The real-analyticity framework and measure-zero argument for injectivity is worked out with unusual rigor and completeness (full proofs for real-analyticity of every architectural component, the zero-set dichotomy theorem, and preservation under GD via the inverse function theorem and absolute continuity of pushforward measures).

SIPIT is a clean, well-specified algorithm with a formal correctness proof and a linear worst-case time bound (T|V|), going beyond prior 'lossless representation' folklore by providing an operational reconstruction procedure.

Large-scale empirical collision search (billions of pairwise comparisons across six model families/sizes, plus an exhaustive near-collision stress test) consistently fails to find collisions, which is at least consistent with the theory.

Related work positioning against Sutter et al. (2025) and Jiang & Haghtalab (2025) is clear and the distinction (last-token state, injectivity w.r.t. parameters, persistence under training) is well articulated.
weaknesses: Critical internal inconsistency: the paper explicitly lists tied embeddings/weight sharing as a failure case that breaks injectivity (Section 2, 'Failure cases'), yet essentially all empirically tested models (GPT-2 family in particular) use tied input/output embeddings by default, and the paper never states whether tying was disabled in the experiments. This calls into question whether the theoretical guarantee actually applies to the models used to 'confirm' it empirically, and the discrepancy is never addressed.

The training-preservation theorem (Theorem 2.3) only covers vanilla (mini-batch) GD with step sizes in (0,1) using exact real-arithmetic parameters; it does not cover Adam/AdamW, momentum, weight decay, dropout, or mixed/low-precision (fp16/bf16/int8) training and inference, which are used in virtually every real LLM pipeline. Since the paper itself treats quantization as a canonical injectivity-breaking operation, the central 'preserved under training' claim may not actually hold for any model trained and deployed the way real LLMs are trained and served — a major disconnect between the theorem's scope and the paper's title/claims about 'language models' in general.

The continuous, real-number measure-zero argument does not straightforwardly transfer to finite-precision floating-point computation, where genuinely distinct real parameter values are routinely rounded to identical floats; the empirical 'no collisions' results use a fixed threshold (1e-6) rather than actually reasoning about float32/bf16 rounding behavior, so the gap between the theory and the deployed numerical reality is not seriously engaged.

The title and framing ('Language Models ARE Injective and Hence Invertible') considerably overstate what is proven: the result is a generic/almost-sure statement that provably fails for common, deliberately-engineered-but-ubiquitous architectural choices (tied embeddings, quantization), yet the abstract and conclusion present injectivity as an essentially unconditional structural fact about 'language models'.

The invertibility experiments (Table 2) are conducted only on GPT-2 Small with short (20-token) sequences and a modest vocabulary; there is no demonstration that SIPIT scales to the large vocabularies (100k+) and long contexts typical of modern deployed LLMs, despite the collision-search experiments being run on larger models — the two experimental threads are not unified on the same models.

Baselines for the inversion experiment are weak: HARDPROMPTS is a method designed for a different (CLIP-based, multimodal) objective and is adapted post hoc without strong justification of fairness, and BRUTEFORCE is essentially a straw-man ablation of SIPIT itself rather than an independent competing method; no comparison is made to more sophisticated (even if approximate) hidden-state inversion baselines.

The practical/legal discussion (e.g., invoking the Hamburg DPA opinion) is somewhat speculative and not carefully scoped to the paper's actual guarantees (which, per the above, may not hold for tied-embedding, low-precision, non-vanilla-GD-trained models), risking overreach in the societal-impact framing.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous, self-contained mathematical treatment (real-analyticity of transformer components, zero-set arguments, inverse function theorem, pushforward/absolute-continuity arguments) to establish almost-sure injectivity both at initialization and after finite-horizon gradient descent, going beyond prior work (e.g., Sutter et al. 2025) that only addressed initialization and full hidden-state matrices rather than the operationally relevant last-token representation.

SIPIT is a genuinely useful algorithmic contribution: it turns the theoretical injectivity claim into a constructive, provably correct (linear-time worst-case) inversion procedure, and the paper supplies a full correctness proof (Theorem D.2) along with a practical gradient-guided policy.

Extensive empirical validation: billions of pairwise collision tests across six model families (GPT-2, Gemma-3, Llama-3.1, Mistral, Phi-4, TinyStories), an exhaustive 343-billion-pair stress test on near-collision candidates, and sequence-length/depth ablations, all consistently showing no collisions and clear separation margins.

SIPIT is empirically compared against reasonable baselines (HardPrompts, brute-force ablation) and shows large efficiency gains while achieving 100% exact recovery, supporting the practical claim of efficient exact inversion.
The writing is generally clear, well-organized, and the appendix is unusually thorough and self-contained, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: The theorems are stated over real-valued parameters and real-analytic maps, but all experiments are run on models with finite-precision (float16/bf16/float32) computation; the paper does not clearly reconcile how the idealized 'almost-sure over continuous distributions' guarantee applies to the discretized, quantized arithmetic actually used in practice, which is precisely where realistic collisions (e.g., due to rounding) could occur.

Many state-of-the-art LMs (including GPT-2, tested here) use weight tying between input and output embeddings, and the paper's own 'failure cases' discussion acknowledges that identical embedding rows break injectivity by construction; the practical relevance of this caveat to the tested models is not thoroughly investigated.

The exhaustive collision search explicitly found 5 near-identical prompt pairs, which is glossed over as 'motivating a question' rather than being analyzed as evidence that separation margins can become arbitrarily small in practice, somewhat undercutting the 'no free privacy' framing.

SIPIT requires full white-box access to model weights and internal hidden states at a chosen layer to run the verifier, which substantially limits the paper's stated privacy/legal implications (an external adversary with only API access could not mount this attack), yet the discussion section frames the privacy implications quite broadly.

The core proof technique (real-analyticity + measure-zero zero-sets + Inverse Function Theorem for preserving absolute continuity under GD) is a fairly standard toolkit in this style of argument and closely parallels contemporaneous work (Sutter et al. 2025; Jiang & Haghtalab 2025), making the incremental novelty (last-token map, training-time persistence) somewhat narrower than the framing suggests.
The HARDPROMPTS baseline was adapted from a vision-language setting to text-only with modified objective/steps, which may not represent a strong or fair comparison for the inversion task.
